Preclude

prih-KLOOD -- the second syllable rhymes with 'rude'. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To preclude to prevent from happening; to make impossible.

The judge ruled that the signed waiver did not preclude the family from filing a lawsuit.

Worked Example

A student breaks his wrist the week before tennis tryouts, and the doctor's order not to grip a racket for six weeks leaves no possible way for him to compete.

The injury precludes his competing -- it does not merely make tryouts harder; it makes them impossible. That is the force of preclude: to shut the door on something before it can happen at all.

How Preclude Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

prevent

prevent: to stop something from happening

forestall

forestall: to head something off by acting ahead of time

bar

bar: to block or forbid, often by rule or authority

Antonyms

allow

allow: to let something happen

enable

enable: to make something possible

How Strong Is It? — forestall → bar → preclude

forestall vs. preclude

forestall vs. preclude: Forestall is narrower and often gentler than preclude -- you forestall one particular problem by acting ahead of it, while something that precludes an outcome makes it impossible altogether.

bar vs. preclude

bar vs. preclude: Bar can sound even more forceful than preclude: preclude often works quietly, as a condition that happens to make something impossible, while bar suggests an explicit block thrown up by a rule or an authority.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pre-

prefix — pre-: before (Latin prae-)

root — clud-/clus-

root — clud-/clus-: to shut, to close (Latin claudere)

Put it together

Put it together: Preclude comes from Latin prae- ('before') plus claudere ('to shut') -- literally 'to shut beforehand.' Something that precludes an outcome closes the door on it in advance, before the possibility ever opens.

Use the root in a new word: include

Use the root in a new word: include: The field trip fee happens to include lunch and the museum ticket.

Root Check

Word Choice

Preclude is the formal, stronger cousin of prevent: it means the possibility is gone entirely. It takes either a thing ('the rain precluded a picnic') or 'from' plus an action ('the rules preclude judges from voting'). If something is merely made harder, it has not been precluded.
